One idea carries the whole piece: a silhouetted ad man falls past skyscraper glass that reflects period advertising. It is specific to its subject and you remember it.

Choreography from frame to frame: he walks in, a close-up of his shoes, he falls past the reflected ads, his body tumbles in close-up, and the piece resolves on him seated with a cigarette. The ending answers the opening, and the fall gets real weight from the scale changes.

The palette is limited and deliberate: flat black silhouette, warm grey ground, and saturated vintage ad imagery as the only colour. Red only marks the first name in each credit, which ties the type to the system.
The credits sit in negative space beside the figure, so the type is placed with the image instead of on top of it like a slide.
Texture is layered: halftone and print-grain advertising is composited behind the window grid, giving it depth and a sense of the period.
gaps: The type works but is restrained. A plain condensed grotesk in red and black has less expressive scale than the image does.
The office interior in the first frame is drawn in a flatter, more generic vector style than the rich collage that follows.
This is close to the ceiling. It could only go further by matching the custom detail of the silhouette work in the backgrounds as well.

tells: It reads as a fable: a crowd of small figures carries a giant fallen stone head, and the ending scatters the figures into a sculptural landscape. It has a story, not just a style.

The frame formats and structures change from shot to shot: a close-up crop of the procession, a wide shot of the head, a harlequin pattern in portrait format, a pattern on a dark ground, then a scattered tableau. This suggests editing and transitions with a rhythm.
The palette is unusual and controlled: ochre, slate blue, coral, blush, mint and charcoal on bone.
It has real texture: dry-brush grain, stipple, gingham and crosshatch fills, and rough edges on the diamonds.
The characters are built from asymmetric, idiosyncratic shapes, not clip-art defaults.
No type is visible, and its absence serves the piece. The story is carried by the image alone, which is right for a poetic short.
gaps: The idea is evocative but less pointed than A's. The meaning of the head and the procession stays loose, so the piece is harder to retell.
There is no typographic layer or title integration, which A uses to bind its system together.
The two pattern interludes risk reading as decorative filler unless the transitions into them are motivated by the story.

tells: The illustration has real texture and character: a twill fabric grain on the red ground, risograph-style stipple on the tiger, elephant and seal, and odd details like the eye-flowers in the border.
The palette is deliberate: oxblood red with teal, ochre and orange. It is committed and consistent.
The frames repeat one composition: a single circus icon centred on the same floral wallpaper. It feels like a series of stickers or a loop set more than a choreographed film.
The motion implied by the frames is mostly swapping one object for the next, with little camera work, scale change or interaction between frames.
No type is visible. Its absence is neutral here, because nothing frames or names the series.
The subject list (tiger, elephant, cannon, seal, strongman barbell) is the expected circus inventory.
gaps: It needs choreography: transitions where one object becomes the next, camera moves, or a cause-and-effect chain, instead of centred objects swapped in a repeated layout.
It needs an idea beyond 'circus objects': a point of view or a narrative that only this piece could have.
Composition should vary from frame to frame through crops, scale contrast and depth, so that each frame works as a poster.

tells: A single, specific idea that only this piece could have: a flat black silhouette falling past skyscrapers covered in period advertising, a Saul Bass / Vertigo-style fall that doubles as a character's moral collapse
The silhouette is cut out against rendered mid-century interiors and translucent ad imagery, so the graphic and photographic layers build density from frame to frame
Clear choreography: back view, then the step, the fall through layered glass, the tumble in close-up, and the resolution in the iconic reclining pose. The ending answers the opening.
Typography is restrained but deliberate: a red/black two-weight credit system used consistently, placed to sit in the negative space the figure leaves
Unusual, period-specific palette (warm grey, black, ad-red, nicotine amber), with grain and transparency that give it real texture
Every frame works as a poster, and the final frame is a recognisable cultural image
gaps: Credit type could be integrated further into the architecture or ads instead of floating as overlays
The interior render in frame 1 is a touch flatter than the collaged fall sequences
The palette could commit even harder in the ad layers, some of which wash out slightly when stacked

tells: A coherent, strange visual world: a procession of small figures carrying a giant classical head and a fish-like log; there is a narrative and a sense of ritual
The scale contrast is staged with care (huge carried objects over a row of tiny people), and composition varies from close crop to wide tableau to pattern field
A deliberate, slightly off palette (ochre, coral, slate blue, mint, charcoal on bone) with consistent grain, dry-brush and halftone textures
Harlequin diamond patterns act as transitions or match-cuts, which shows thought about how frames connect
No type is visible; the piece is purely image-led and the absence works, with no loss to the work
gaps: The idea is more mood than a sharp concept; it needs a payoff or turn as memorable as A's fall-to-recline
The pattern-interstitial frames (3, 4) are decorative and add less meaning than the narrative frames
No typographic layer or title integration; a considered title moment would lift it to award level

tells: Hand-crafted illustration with real material: a fabric or twill texture on the red ground, grain and stipple on the tiger, elephant and seal, and a folk-art floral pattern with eye motifs

No type is visible; this is acceptable for an ident or loop series, but nothing replaces the type as a structuring device
gaps: Every frame uses one centred-icon layout; vary scale, cropping and depth and let objects interact across cuts
Needs a narrative or transformational idea (e.g. one object morphing into the next) rather than a catalogue of circus props
Introduce a typographic or title component with a point of view to anchor the piece
